# Ecclesiastes 12 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — *"Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come and the years approach of which you will say, 'I find no pleasure in them'"*

**Traditional Reading — The Call to Youth**

This verse marks a major transition from the joy-and-warning tone of chapter 11 to the sobering portrait of aging and death that follows in vv. 2–7. The command to "remember" (*zakar*) is not mere mental recall but a call to active, wholehearted commitment — to love, serve, fear, and obey God. The Septuagint renders it as an aorist imperative ("Just Do It!"). The exhortation to fear God and keep His commandments in vv. 13–14 spells out what "remembering" means. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-12-commentary)

The word "Creator" appears here as a Hebrew plural form (*bara'*), suggesting majesty and greatness. This is the first and only time in Ecclesiastes that God is explicitly named "Creator." The title pivots the whole book away from ignoring accountability to the eternal God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

Gill notes that the plural "Creators" points to the involvement of Father, Son, and Spirit in creation (cf. Gen 1:26; Job 35:10), and that "remembering" includes loving, fearing, and worshipping God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that some (Gratz) proposed reading "cistern" or "fountain" instead of "Creator" — referring to a wife (Prov 5:15–18) — but this alteration has no support. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

**"Days of adversity" / "evil days"** — these are not ethical evil but physical hardship: sickness, sorrow, senility, and eventually dying. The warning is: don't wait until old age to turn to God, when the capacity for joy may be lost. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-12-commentary)

**"I find no pleasure in them"** — Gill references Barzillai at eighty (2 Sam 19:35), who could no longer taste food, hear singing, or discern good from evil. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

**Tradition-Specific Notes:**
- **Baptist (Gill):** Sees the plural "Creators" as a Trinitarian hint. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)
- **Reformed/Evangelical (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasises the "plural of majesty" reading and the pivot from under-the-sun thinking to eternal accountability. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)
- **Precept Austin (broadly evangelical):** Stresses that only believers can truly obey this command, since fallen flesh defaults away from God (Rom 3:11). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-12-commentary)

---

## v. 2 — *"before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain"*

**Traditional Reading**

Two major lines of interpretation exist for the whole section vv. 2–7: (1) it depicts the effects of a violent storm on a house and its inhabitants, or (2) it is a figurative description of the decay of the aging human body. Most traditional commentators favour the latter — the "allegory of old age." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

The darkening of sun, moon, and stars pictures the fading of joy, clarity, and vitality as old age advances. "Clouds return after the rain" means one storm (one affliction) follows another with no respite — unlike youth, where sunshine and storm alternate. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

Gill sees the sun and moon as the superior and inferior faculties of the soul — understanding, mind, judgment, will, and affections — and the stars as bright notions fixed in memory, all impaired in old age. The "clouds returning" are catarrhs, defluxions, and rheums flowing one after another, or simply the perpetual succession of disorders. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary summarises: fading hopes and repeated sorrows accompanying advancing age, symbolised by darkness obscuring heavenly lights. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

**Modern Scholarship:** The Precept Austin notes that there is "disagreement on the interpretation of this verse" but, read in context, it is best understood as a metaphorical description of how joy and clarity wane as death approaches. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-12-commentary)

---

## v. 3 — *"on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop, when those grinding cease because they are few and those watching through windows see dimly"*

**Traditional Reading — The Body as a House**

The human body is depicted as a house (cf. Job 4:19; 2 Cor 5:1; 2 Pet 1:13–14). Each image represents a body part in decay:

- **"Keepers of the house tremble"** — the arms and hands, which guard and work for the body, now shake with palsy. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm) Gill adds that some (Targum) think of the knees, while Midrash and Jarchi say the ribs, but Aben Ezra and most favour the hands and arms. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Strong men stoop"** — the legs, thighs, and knees, once pillars of marble, now bend and sag. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"Those grinding cease because they are few"** — the teeth. The Hebrew word is feminine ("grinding maidens") because grinding was women's work. They become few, straggling, and can no longer perform their office. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"Those watching through windows see dimly"** — the eyes, looking out from their sockets like watchers from windows. The eyelashes or eyelids are the lattice. The Pulpit Commentary cites Cicero, *De Nat. Deor.* 2.140, on eyes as "watchers" placed in the highest position. Moses at 120 was the great exception (Deut 34:7). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

**Caveat:** Ellicott warns that while the general impression is clear, attempts to find precise anatomical explanations for every image become forced; some prefer to see v. 3 as only a general description of consternation from a gathering tempest. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

---

## v. 4 — *"when the doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades away, when one rises at the sound of a bird and all the daughters of song grow faint"*

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Doors to the street are shut"** — the lips, the "double doors" of the mouth (dual form in Hebrew). The mouth closes because teeth are gone; the aged person mumbles both in speaking and eating. Cf. Ps 141:3, "door of my lips." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm) Gill also notes that the aged stay indoors, not caring to go out because of infirmities. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Sound of the mill fades away"** — the noise of chewing is low when teeth are lost; also the voice becomes lower. In the ancient world, the sound of grinding betokened cheerfulness and prosperity; its cessation was ominous (Jer 25:10; Rev 18:22). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"One rises at the sound of a bird"** — the Pulpit Commentary calls this "a very difficult sentence." The usual reading: the old man sleeps so lightly that even a bird's chirp wakes him. However, this breaks the figurative consistency. An alternative: the old man's own voice becomes a "childish treble," piping like a bird — as the larynx muscles relax. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm) Gill adds: the aged person rises early at cock-crow, going to bed soon and waking at the least noise. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"All the daughters of song grow faint"** — the organs of speech and hearing. The old man can neither sing nor enjoy singing (cf. Barzillai, 2 Sam 19:35). The Pulpit Commentary references Juvenal, *Satire* 10, and Shakespeare's *As You Like It* (Act 2, Scene 7): "His big, manly voice, turning again toward childish treble, pipes and whistles in his sound." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

Ellicott remarks simply: "all communication with the outer world broken off; the double doors towards the street shut, the cheerful noise of grinding not heard without." He notes that "no satisfactory explanation" of "he shall rise up at the voice of the bird" has been given. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

---

## v. 5 — *"when men fear the heights and dangers of the road, when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring, and the caper berry shrivels — for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets."*

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Fear the heights and dangers of the road"** — the old man is afraid to climb (shortness of breath, muscular weakness) and fearful of stumbling on every little stone. Some see here also the *via dolorosa* of dying — the steep ascent the soul must travel. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"The almond tree blossoms"** — white/grey hair. The almond tree blossoms in winter on a leafless stem; its pale pink flowers turn snowy white as they fall. The Hebrew word *shaked* also means "to hasten," suggesting the hastening of old age and death. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm) Gill adds: the hoary head, like the almond blossom, looks beautiful and is venerable when found in the way of righteousness (Lev 19:32). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"The grasshopper loses its spring"** — several interpretations compete. The lightest burden (even a grasshopper) troubles the aged. Or: the locust, an Eastern delicacy, is loathed (appetite gone). Delitzsch (followed by some Jewish interpreters) sees the locust as a figure for the hip joint or *caput femoris*, which loses its spring-like elasticity. The Septuagint renders it "the locust grows fat," which some take as depicting corpulence or dropsical swelling in old age. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"The caper berry shrivels"** (BSB "caper berry"; KJV "desire shall fail") — the caper berry was highly regarded as an appetite stimulant and aphrodisiac. Its failure pictures the loss of all desire — for food, for bodily pleasures, for sexual intimacy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/) Ellicott confirms: "the caper berry (translated 'desire' in our version) fails." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"Man goes to his eternal home"** — the grave, "the house of his world" or "the long home." The Hebrew phrase can mean "his eternal house." The Preacher sets aging and death in connection with eternity, not meaninglessness — a crucial turn from the "under the sun" premise. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/) Gill notes that the Targum calls it "the grave" and that Cicero called it the "eternal house." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Mourners walk the streets"** — the professional mourners (men and women hired for the purpose) or the grieving relatives processing toward burial. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

---

## v. 6 — *"Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed, before the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well"*

**Traditional Reading**

Four metaphors for the moment of death — all conveying something precious, functional, and irreparable being destroyed:

- **"Silver cord is snapped"** — The Targum takes this as the tongue being silenced. More widely, Jewish interpreters (Midrash, Jarchi) understand it as the spinal cord — the marrow descending like a silver cord from the brain down the backbone, from which nerves and sinews spring. "Silver" from its colour (white even after death) and its preciousness. When "loosed," paralysis follows, the immediate forerunner of death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Golden bowl is crushed"** — the skull, or more precisely the *pia mater* (the membrane containing the brain). Called a "bowl" from its form, "golden" from its preciousness and colour. When it "runs back" (dries, shrinks, breaks), all animal motion ceases. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Pitcher shattered at the spring"** — the heart, the fountain of life, with its two cavities (ventricles) from which veins and arteries carry blood throughout the body. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Wheel broken at the well"** — the circulatory system or the respiratory organs, pictured as the wheel that draws up water. When it breaks, the body's life-sustaining processes cease.

Guzik quotes Eaton: "The image points to the value of life (silver… gold), and the drama in the end of a life whose pieces cannot be put together again." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

Ellicott admits frankly: "After using all the help my predecessors have given me, I frankly own myself unable to give more than a vague account of the figures employed in this whole passage." Yet he notes that English readers have always been deeply impressed by vv. 6–7 as speaking of "the dissolution of the noble structure of the bodily frame." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

---

## v. 7 — *"before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it"*

**Traditional Reading**

This verse is seen across all traditions as a strong, clear affirmation of life after death — remarkable in an Old Testament context. The body returns to dust (Gen 3:19), but the spirit returns to God for judgment and eternal reckoning.

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that this repeats the teaching of Eccl 3:21 and that "future details are not given here but are recognized in Proverbs 14:32; Proverbs 11:7 and clearly affirmed in Luke 23:43; Luke 16:22–31; 2 Corinthians 5:1." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

Guzik writes: "This is why it is so important to remember your Creator in this life; because when this life is over, one will answer to the eternal God and to eternity." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

The Bible.org (Bob Utley) notes call this "a strong affirmation" in light of Qoheleth's questioning of all things. (https://bible.org/seriespage/ecclesiastes-12)

The Catholic Answers summary notes that God "will judge their actions when the body turns into the dust from which it came and the spirit returns to God its maker." (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/ecclesiastes)

---

## v. 8 — *"'Futility of futilities,' says the Teacher. 'Everything is futile!'"*

**Traditional Reading**

This is the book's inclusio — matching Eccl 1:2. By way of contrast, the Preacher returns to his starting point. Under the "under the sun" premise (excluding eternity and the eternal God), life is not merely meaningless but the ultimate in meaninglessness. Guzik cites Viktor Frankl (holocaust survivor and author of *Man's Search for Meaning*) as a modern illustration of the despair of a life without transcendent meaning. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

The Bible.org commentary observes: "This looks like a concluding summary statement, matching 1:2. One wonders how many conclusions were originally a part of Ecclesiastes and how many were added later." (https://bible.org/seriespage/ecclesiastes-12)

**Modern Scholarship:** Desiring God (John Piper's ministry) notes that "*hebel*" (translated "vanity" or "futility") "might better be translated as 'enigmatic' or 'perplexing'" rather than "meaninglessness," and that "'under the sun,' which occurs 28 times, may not mean, 'Well, this is a portrayal of the world as it is without God,' … but rather, maybe it means a world where we can't see all that God is doing." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/where-is-providence-in-the-vanity-of-ecclesiastes)

---

## vv. 9–10 — *"Not only was the Teacher wise, but he also taught the people knowledge; he pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs. The Teacher searched to find delightful sayings and to record accurate words of truth."*

**Traditional Reading**

These verses (the epilogue) are generally understood as a third-person commendation of the Preacher (Qoheleth/Solomon). The Preacher did not merely accumulate wisdom for himself — he actively taught the people, carefully pondering, researching, and arranging proverbs. He sought both delightful (pleasing, acceptable) words and accurate, upright words of truth — the two characteristics balancing each other. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

Ellicott states his conviction "that the epilogue which here follows is an integral part of the book" and that "the writer, who has up to this recorded the words of Kohéleth, now speaks in his own name, and informs his readers that the preacher … was also a writer, and the author of the well-known Proverbs." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds that the order indicates Solomon "gave careful thought to the need of man, searched for that which was suitable, then arranged it in the order that would best accomplish his purpose." Knowledge here "includes reverence, understanding and wisdom, not just an accumulation of facts" (Prov 1:7; 9:10). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

---

## v. 11 — *"The words of the wise are like goads, and the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd."*

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Like goads"** — sharp sticks used to prod oxen. The words of the wise spur the will, prompt action, and sometimes cause discomfort to move the hearer in the right direction.

- **"Like firmly embedded nails"** — well-driven nails that stick in the memory and provide a fixed, firm anchor for teaching.

- **"Driven by a single Shepherd"** — all true wisdom ultimately comes from one source: God, the Shepherd of Israel (Ps 80:1). This is widely taken as an acknowledgment of divine inspiration. "Special confidence was appropriate in those words given by one Shepherd, even if they came through a wise man or a scholar." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary explicitly connects this to 2 Peter 1:21 on the inspiration of Scripture: "They are from 'one shepherd', God above, though delivered by Solomon." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew words are "enigmatical, and one cannot feel great confidence in assigning their precise meaning." The word "masters" has appeared earlier as "master of the tongue" (10:11) and "master of wings" (10:20). "Assemblies" could mean collections of sayings as well as gatherings of people. The last clause means that "the sages … have been given for the instruction of the people by Israel's great Shepherd." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

Guzik quotes Kidner: "Here then are two more qualities that mark the pointed sayings of the wise: they spur the will and stick in the memory." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

---

## v. 12 — *"And by these, my son, be further warned: There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body."*

**Traditional Reading**

A caution against endless reading of human writings. Not everything written comes from the "one Shepherd." The wise reader should be admonished by the divinely-inspired words (v. 11) and not be swallowed up by the endless production of books. Adam Clarke remarked (cited in Guzik): "Two thousand years have elapsed since this was written; and since that time some millions of treatises have been added, on all kinds of subjects … The press is still groaning under and teeming with books, books innumerable." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

Guzik also quotes Kidner: "We grow addicted to research itself, in love with our own hard questions. An answer would spoil everything." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary sees this as a warning "against the many profitless books that are not from the one Divine source," citing Isa 19:11–16; 2 Thess 3:14; Rom 16:17–18; 1 Tim 6:20. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

Ellicott notes that the word "study" occurs only here in the Old Testament, though it is not a Talmudic word. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

---

## v. 13 — *"When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man."*

**Traditional Reading**

This is the grand conclusion of the entire book. After all the searching, all the "under the sun" experiments, all the wrestling with life's enigmas, the Preacher lands here.

- **"Fear God"** — a reverential trust and awe that puts all other fears, hopes, and admirations in their proper place (Kidner, cited by Guzik). It "includes the whole of internal religion, or powerful godliness; all the graces of the Spirit … reverence of God, love to him, faith in him, and in his Son Jesus Christ; hope of eternal life from him; humility of soul, patience and submission to his will." (Gill, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

- **"Keep His commandments"** — the fruit and evidence of fearing God. This is the only place in Ecclesiastes where "the commands of God" are mentioned (Eaton, cited by Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

- **"This is the whole duty of man"** — The BSB and most modern translations note that "duty" is not in the Hebrew. The phrase reads literally: "this is the whole of the man" or "this is man's all." Eaton (cited by Guzik) says the idiom means "this applies to everyone" (cf. Eccl 3:13; 5:19). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/) Ellicott agrees: "Rather, the duty of every man. The sacred writer practically anticipates the teaching of Romans 3:29." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

- **"From that to this should be every man's pilgrimage … We begin at vanity, and never know perfectly that we are vain till we come to fear God and keep his commandments"** (Trapp, cited by Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

**Catholic Reading:** The Catholic Encyclopedia summarises: "In the epilogue Qoheleth again lays stress upon his authority as the teacher of wisdom, and declares that the pith of his teaching is: Fear God and keep the Commandments; for that is the whole man." (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05244b.htm)

---

## v. 14 — *"For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil."*

**Traditional Reading**

The final motivation: an eschatological judgment in which everything — even every secret thing — will be brought to light and judged.

Ellicott writes one of the strongest statements on this verse: "Considering that the book is filled with complaints of the imperfection of earthly retribution, this announcement of a tribunal, at which 'every work,' 'every secret thing,' shall be brought into judgment, cannot be reasonably understood of anything but a judgment after this life; so that this book, after all its sceptical debatings, ends by enunciating, more distinctly than is done elsewhere in the Old Testament, the New Testament doctrine of a day when God shall judge the secrets of men (Romans 2:16), shall bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and make manifest the counsels of the hearts (1 Corinthians 4:5)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/12.htm)

Gill concurs: "Not in this life, but in the day of the great judgment, as the Targum explains it … all being observed and taken notice of by the omniscient God, who has registered them in the book of his remembrance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

Guzik ties it back to the whole book's argument: "This is the complete opposite of believing that all is vanity or meaningless; it means that everything has meaning and importance, both for the present and for eternity. 'If God cares as much as this, nothing can be pointless' (Kidner)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-12/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that while judgment applies to all, "the Bible teaches elsewhere that saved and unsaved will be judged, at different times" (Rom 14:10; Rev 20:11–12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-12.html)

---

## Summary of Where Traditions Differ

**Little disagreement on the main message.** All consulted traditions — Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes), Reformed/Evangelical (Guzik, Precept Austin), and Catholic (Haydock, Catholic Encyclopedia) — agree that chapter 12 calls the young to remember God before old age and death, describes aging in poetic allegory, and concludes that fearing God and keeping His commandments is humanity's whole purpose in light of coming judgment.

**Minor variations:**
- **"Creator" as plural:** Baptist (Gill) sees a Trinitarian intimation. Reformed (Guzik) emphasises "plural of majesty." Both readings coexist in evangelicalism.
- **"One Shepherd" (v. 11):** All evangelical traditions see this as God. Ellicott (Anglican) connects it to "Israel's great Shepherd" (Ps 80:1).
- **"Whole duty of man" vs. "man's all" (v. 13):** Traditional translations (KJV) added "duty." Modern evangelical scholarship (Guzik/Eaton) and Ellicott agree the Hebrew idiom means "this applies to every man" or "this is the whole of man."
- **Ecclesiastes' "vanity" (v. 8):** Desiring God (Reformed Baptist perspective) suggests *hebel* may be better rendered "enigmatic" or "perplexing" than "meaningless." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/where-is-providence-in-the-vanity-of-ecclesiastes)

**Catholic and Orthodox:** The Catholic Encyclopedia reading aligns substantially with Protestant ones — the book's end is "Fear God and keep the Commandments." The Orthodox tradition (oca.org) was searched but no distinct verse-by-verse Orthodox commentary on Ecclesiastes 12 could be retrieved from the permitted sites.

**Modern Scholarship:** The NET Bible notes (cited at Precept Austin) observe that vv. 1–7 comprise "one long sentence in Hebrew," and that the word "evil" in v. 1 refers to physical hardship, not moral evil. Bible.org raises the question of whether multiple conclusions were originally part of Ecclesiastes (a redaction-critical observation). (https://bible.org/seriespage/ecclesiastes-12)

**Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal/Anglican distinctives:** Searches on lcms.org, 1517.org, seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu, and samstorms.org did not return verse-specific denominational content distinct from the general evangelical consensus represented above. No prosperity/Word of Faith or hyper-grace teaching on Ecclesiastes 12 was found in the permitted sites.
